learning_outcomes: Conditions and accounting treatment for changes in accounting policies
Accounting policies generally applicable to non-life insurance business
key_takeaways: Accounting policies are specific principles, bases, conventions, rules, and practices applied in preparing and presenting financial statements[cite: 1].

The primary objectives of accounting policies are maintaining financial quality, ensuring reliability, preserving consistency, enabling comparability, and guaranteeing full and fair disclosure[cite: 1].

An entity cannot change its accounting policy arbitrarily; a change is permitted only: (1) to comply with statutory law[cite: 1], (2) to comply with an Accounting Standard[cite: 1], or (3) to provide a truer and fairer view of financial statements[cite: 1].
A voluntary change in an accounting policy must normally be accounted for retrospectively, adjusting past-period surplus or deficiency in the current P&L[cite: 1].
Under AS 1, all significant accounting policies and any material changes (with quantified financial impact) must be disclosed in the Notes to Accounts[cite: 1].
In non-life insurance accounting, the Reserve for Unexpired Risk is maintained at 100% of Net Written Premium for Marine Hull, and 50% (or 1/365th) for other domestic business classes[cite: 1].
A Premium Deficiency Reserve (PDR) is mandatory if expected claims and expenses exceed the unearned premium reserve[cite: 1].

Insurers must formulate clear policy disclosures on the segregation and apportionment of investment income and management expenses between Policyholders' funds (Revenue A/c) and Shareholders' funds (P&L A/c)[cite: 1].

self_test_questions.question: The term 'accounting policies' refers to:
options: The measurement bases used by an entity[cite: 1]
The accounting concepts and conventions adopted by an entity[cite: 1]
The accounting principles applied by an entity[cite: 1]
self_test_questions.explanation: Accounting policies encompass specific principles, measurement bases, conventions, and rules applied by an enterprise in financial reporting[cite: 1].

self_test_questions.question: When can an entity change one of its accounting policies?
options: Whenever it wishes to do so[cite: 1]
If this would result in the provision of reliable and more relevant information[cite: 1]
If this would reduce the cost of preparing the financial statements[cite: 1]
self_test_questions.correct_answer: If this would result in the provision of reliable and more relevant information
self_test_questions.explanation: An accounting policy change is valid only to comply with statute, new standards, or if it produces more reliable and relevant (truer/fairer) information[cite: 1].

self_test_questions.question: Reserve for unexpired risk is statutorily created at what percentage for marine hull business?
self_test_questions.explanation: IRDAI mandates a 100% Reserve for Unexpired Risk on Marine Hull business, whereas other classes use 50% or the 1/365th basis[cite: 1].

self_test_questions.question: A change in an accounting policy not resulting from the initial application of a standard must normally be accounted for:
options: Prospectively, unless it is impracticable to account for impact of change[cite: 1]
self_test_questions.explanation: Non-mandatory policy modifications must be accounted for retrospectively with quantified impact disclosed in Notes to Accounts[cite: 1].

self_test_questions.question: In foreign currency transactions, monetary and non-monetary assets and liabilities of non-integral foreign operations are translated at the:
self_test_questions.explanation: Assets and liabilities (including contingent liabilities) of non-integral foreign operations are translated at the closing exchange rate[cite: 1].
